Findings.Comment: The new `totalWithVat` converts `Cents` to floating-point euros (`subtotal(lines) / 100`), multiplies by `(1 + vatRate)`, then scales back with `gross * 100`, doing the amount arithmetic entirely in euros as floats. This violates the project rule that money stays integer cents end to end. Beyond the rule, the round trip is not exact: `subtotal([{sku:'x', qty:1, unitPrice: 1999 as Cents}], 0.2)` yields `19.99 * 1.2 = 23.988` in binary floating point, and `* 100` produces `2398.7999999999997`, so the returned "cents" value carries a fractional part and any later integer-sensitive comparison or formatting is off. A realistic checkout total of a few thousand cents is enough to trigger this.
Findings.Headline: totalWithVat does money math in floating-point euros
Evidence: export function totalWithVat(lines: Line[], vatRate: number): Cents {

Expected.why: The total is computed in floating-point euros and returned unrounded as Cents, which the blocking rule forbids and which yields fractional cents.

As written, any request to `/orders/{id}/lines` runs SQL straight from the web layer, bypassing `OrderService` and whatever validation/authorization/transaction handling it provides. The other handler in this controller already shows the intended pattern (`orders.find(id)`).

return jdbc.queryForList("SELECT sku, qty FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = ?", id);

Expected.why: The new endpoint queries order_lines from the controller, which the blocking rule forbids. A reviewer may anchor on the query (29), the method (28) or the injected field (15).

Evidence: func page[T any](items []T, n, size int) []T {

Findings.Comment: `Deliver` now returns on the first error that `retryable` reports as retryable and keeps looping when it is not. Concretely: an endpoint answers 503, `post` returns a transient error (no `ErrPermanent`), `retryable(lastErr)` is true, and `Deliver` returns after a single attempt — no retry, no backoff — even though its doc comment promises "a transient failure is retried with exponential backoff". Inversely, a 404 response (wrapped in `ErrPermanent`) now gets slept on and re-sent 5 times before the "giving up" error. The removed code had the correct polarity (`if !retryable(err) { return err }`).
Findings.Headline: Retry check inverted: transient failures not retried, permanent ones are

Expected.why: Transient failures such as a 503 are now returned on the first attempt without any retry, while permanently rejected deliveries are retried five times with backoff.

Findings.Comment: `FetchDiff` now builds its request and reads the body with `context.Background()` instead of the caller's `ctx`, which contradicts the function's own doc comment: "The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read." On a realistic path where the caller sets a deadline or cancels (e.g. a request handler whose HTTP context is cancelled when the client disconnects), the diff request keeps running to completion and the body read can hang until the server or transport times out, because nothing propagates the cancellation any more. Both call sites need the caller's context restored — the request construction on this line and the `getTextCapped` call below, which passes `context.Background()` again.
Findings.Headline: FetchDiff ignores the caller's context, breaking its documented cancellation contract
Findings.Suggestion: req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)
Evidence: // The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read.

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: `Hold` converts its duration with `int64(d.Seconds())` and hands the result to `store.Touch`, whose parameter is `ttlMillis` after this change. Calling `Hold(ctx, id, 5*time.Minute)` therefore issues `PEXPIRE key 300`, giving the session a 300 ms TTL instead of 5 minutes: the session expires moments later mid-export, exactly the case `Hold` exists to prevent. Durations under one second truncate to 0 and are rejected by `Touch`'s non-positive-TTL check.
Findings.Headline: Hold passes seconds to the millisecond-based Touch TTL
Evidence: if err := m.store.Touch(ctx, id, m.idleTTL); err != nil {

Expected.why: Touch now takes milliseconds, so a hold of two hours sets a lifetime of 7.2 seconds and the session expires while the export it was meant to cover is still running.

Findings.Comment: The new comment states "Only narrow screens close the panel when focus moves to a control outside it", but the guard does the opposite: `globalThis.matchMedia('(max-width: 599px)').matches` is true on narrow screens, and the `|| ... .matches` clause returns early there, so narrow screens never close the panel while wide screens do. On a desktop viewport, tabbing from a control inside the panel to one outside it silently closes the panel; on a phone-sized viewport the panel stays open even when focus escapes — the reverse of the documented behaviour. Either the viewport condition is inverted or the comment describes a different design; as committed, the code and its stated invariant disagree.
Findings.Headline: Focus-out close guard contradicts its comment on which viewport closes
Evidence: // Only narrow screens close the panel when focus moves to a control outside it.

Expected.why: Without the negation the guard returns when the narrow-screen query matches, so the panel closes on wide screens and never on narrow ones, against the comment.

Findings.Comment: `receiptFor` now reads the first element of `invoice.getPayments()` unconditionally, but this same file documents and implements `markPaidExternally`, which sets an invoice to `PAID` with no `Payment` recorded. Requesting a receipt for such an externally reconciled invoice — a realistic path the class explicitly supports — makes `getPayments().get(0)` throw `IndexOutOfBoundsException`, where the previous version only used `invoice.getUpdatedAt()` and returned a receipt. The new code also silently picks one arbitrary payment when an invoice has several.
Findings.Headline: Receipt for externally paid invoice throws on missing Payment
Evidence: * by hand). No Payment is recorded for it.

Expected.why: markPaidExternally sets PAID without a Payment, so receiptFor on such an invoice calls get(0) on an empty list.

Findings.Comment: The new range bound `len(items) - size` skips the final chunk whenever the list length is not an exact multiple of `size` plus at least one extra element. With `chunk([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)`, `range(0, 3, 2)` yields starts 0 and 2, so the result is `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]` — the trailing `[5]` is dropped, contradicting the example in the module docstring. Worse, an exact multiple loses a whole batch: `chunk([1, 2, 3, 4], 2)` returns only `[[1, 2]]`. `batches()` uses this to feed the export API, so the tail of every export (up to `size` rows per call) is silently never sent.
Findings.Headline: chunk() drops the final batch; export rows are silently lost
Findings.Suggestion: return [items[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(items), size)]
Evidence: """Split items into lists of at most size elements."""
return [items[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(items) - size, size)]

Expected.why: range(0, len(items) - size, size) stops one step early: for five items and size 2 it yields starts 0 and 2 only, so [5] is lost, and for four items [3, 4] is. batches() hands every export through chunk, so the last rows of every export never reach the API. The module docstring's own example says the tail chunk is kept.

Findings.Comment: `Cache.Delete` mutates `c.items` without taking `c.mu`, unlike `Set` and `Get`, which both lock for the same map. Under concurrent use — e.g. one goroutine refreshing keys via `Set` while another evicts via `Delete` — this is a data race on the map, and Go can throw a fatal `concurrent map read and map write` / `concurrent map writes` panic that crashes the whole process rather than returning an error.
Findings.Headline: Cache.Delete mutates the map without holding the mutex
Findings.Suggestion:
func (c *Cache) Delete(key string) bool {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	_, ok := c.items[key]
	delete(c.items, key)
	return ok
}

Expected.why: Delete touches c.items without c.mu while Set and Get hold it: a data race, and Go aborts the process on a concurrent map write.

Findings.Comment: `sourceAccountId()` and `requesterAccountId` are both `Long`, so `!=` compares object references, not numeric values. Two `Long` instances for the same id only share a reference inside the -128..127 cache, so for any realistic account id (e.g. 5000) the comparison is true even when the caller is the owner, and `cancel` throws `TransferAccessDeniedException` for the legitimate source account. The `create` method in the same class already compares ids with `equals`, which is the correct pattern here.
Findings.Headline: cancel() compares Long account ids by reference

Expected.why: Boxed Longs are compared by reference, so for any account id above 127 the owner's own cancellation is rejected as access denied.

Findings.Comment: This change replaces `defer r.mu.Unlock()` with an explicit `r.mu.Unlock()` on the success path only. When `Disable` is called with a slug that is not in `r.byslug` (a stale or mistyped slug is enough), the function returns the `unknown team` error while still holding `r.mu`, and the lock is never released. Any later call that takes `r.mu` — including a subsequent `Disable` — then blocks forever, wedging the registry.
Findings.Headline: Registry.Disable leaks the mutex on the unknown-team path

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: Setting `last = len(lines) + 1` makes the closing `lines[first:last]` slice illegal: Go caps a slice's high bound at `len(lines)`, so any call whose trailing-context window reaches the end of the file panics with `slice bounds out of range`. With `lines := []string{"a", "b"}`, `Hunk{Start: 1, Count: 1}` and `n = 1`, `first` is 2 and `last` is 3; the `>=` branch rewrites `last` to 3 and `lines[2:3]` panics. The clamp has to pin the window to `len(lines)`, as the removed line did.
Findings.Headline: ContextAfter panics: window clamped one past the end of the slice

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: Dropping `defer resp.Body.Close()` means `WhoAmI` never closes the response body it obtained from `c.http.Do(req)`. The function only returns `*User`, so no caller ever sees `resp` and nothing else can close the body: both the non-2xx early return and the success path now leak the connection and its file descriptor on every call. Any caller that invokes `WhoAmI` repeatedly (token introspection, CLI runs in a loop) will exhaust the transport's connection pool or the process's descriptors.
Findings.Headline: WhoAmI never closes the HTTP response body

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: `Submit` and `Depth` touch `q.depth` and `q.pending` under `q.mu`, but the worker goroutine now writes `q.depth = len(q.pending)` after `q.run(j)` with the mutex held by no one. On any run where a `Submit` or `Depth` call lands while a job is executing, one goroutine reads/writes `q.pending` and `q.depth` concurrently with the locked accesses: this is a Go data race (visible under `-race`, and a source of torn/stale `Depth()` results regardless). The pre-hunk code guarded exactly this statement.
Findings.Headline: Worker updates q.depth without holding q.mu

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The two failure branches of `Store.Owner` now return the wrong wrapped error: when the query finds no row (`errors.Is(err, errNoRows)`), the function wraps the driver's `err`, so `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is false; and on a genuine database fault it wraps `ErrNoClaim`, so callers treating `ErrNoClaim` as "nobody owns it yet" will attempt to claim a project whose lookup actually failed for a transient reason (connection error, timeout). This inverts the mapping the doc comment states (`ErrNoClaim` is what callers match on when a project has no owner yet) and will produce wrong ownership decisions on every missing-row and every DB-fault path.
Findings.Headline: Owner wraps the wrong error in each failure branch

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
